# Between regulation, pressure and collaboration: the public-private entanglement in content moderation

## Abstract

This paper examines the evolving roles of states in content moderation and their complex relationships with social media platforms over time. As these platforms have become central to global communication, their interactions with governments have shaped content moderation in increasingly intricate ways. Despite the significance of these relationships, their chronological development and their implications remain insufficiently explored. This paper addresses this gap through an analysis of the annual reports of the United Nations' Special Rapporteurs (SRs) on freedom of opinion and expression from 1995 to 2024. It traces the progressive entanglement between states and platforms, highlighting how governments have increasingly relied on platforms to enforce content moderation through both formal and informal mechanisms. The paper makes two key contributions: first, it provides a chronological account of how state involvement in content moderation has evolved; second, it categorizes types of state-platform relationships, distinguishing between formal and informal modes of influence as well as top-down, bottom-up, and collaborative interactions. Finally, it touches upon the geopolitical issues relating to state--platform relationships in a context where it is unclear whether platforms and governments share the same values of freedom and democracy anymore. By offering an empirical and chronological perspective, this study contributes to ongoing debates on platform governance and the issue of social media regulation.

## Introduction

The recent suspension of the social media platform X in Brazil (Da Silva & Buschschlüter, 2024) and the European Union's investigation into TikTok for alleged algorithmic interference in the Romanian elections (European Commission, 2024) contrast sharply with Mark Zuckerberg's announcement ending fact-checking on the Meta platforms (McMahon, Kleinman, & Subramanian, 2025) and US Vice President Vance's assertion that EU regulations threaten free speech (Atkinson, 2025) . These events illustrate two conflicting visions for regulating social media platforms, marking 2025 as a potential new turning point in the debate on content moderation and state intervention, and widening a divide within the transatlantic legal community (Fahey & Curtin, 2014) . The regulation of social media platforms has been an eventful discussion shaped by their growing role and use as a forum for communication. Indeed, platforms are used by individuals to exchange opinions and 'play a vital role in the realization of important public values and policy objectives (…), including freedom of expression, diversity, public safety, transparency, and socio-economic equality' (Helberger et al., 2018, p. 1) . At the same time, social media platforms act as gatekeepers for individuals (Shoemaker & Vos, 2009) , as they moderate their content for economic, legal, and political reasons, thereby regulating user discourse (DeNardis & Hackl, 2015; Gillespie, 2018) . This dual function complicates the regulatory landscape because state regulation of content moderation always constitutes a form of meta-regulation (Coglianese & Mendelson, 2010) that is overlaid upon a self-regulatory regime.

The regulatory governance of content moderation varies across regions, in the absence of a global regulator or an overarching regulatory framework (Grygiel & Brown, 2019) . The EU has adopted an incremental approach, starting with co-regulatory processes (Marsden, 2011 (Marsden, , 2022)) , such as codes of conduct, and moving towards a hard governance response (Maggetti, 2015) , culminating in the 2022 Digital Services Act (DSA), which imposes strict obligations regarding how platforms must moderate content (Husovec, 2024; Fasel & Weerts, 2024) . In contrast, the U.S. have chosen not to change the liability exemption regime of Section 230 since 1996 (Goldman, 2019) , relying instead on informal engagements between government officials and U.S. platforms (Lee Myers & McCabe, 2023) . The reason for this more conciliatory approach is that social media platforms are viewed as tools of U.S. soft power abroad and as channels for disseminating state media domestically (Grygiel & Sager, 2020) , and U.S. officials and politicians therefore believe they should not be constrained by regulation. In contrast, the relationship with foreign platforms is markedly different. In this regard, there is a clear continuity in the approach of the last three administrations toward TikTok: initially viewed as a threat to national security by the first Trump administration, its forced sale was later formalized in law by the Biden administration, and subsequently pursued by the second Trump administration -all of this on the grounds that the platform serves Chinese interests (Maheshwari & Holpuch, 2025) .

This divergence in regulatory strategies highlights that the regulatory governance of content moderation does not follow a strictly top-down approach (Black, 2002) but rather follows a horizontal model that includes diverse mechanisms of interaction and collaboration between states and platforms. These interactions raise concerns regarding democracy and the rule of law, particularly when states exert pressure on platforms to remove content while avoiding direct legal responsibility (Bambauer, 2015) . In the U.S., these concerns have led to judicial scrutiny, including a Supreme Court case addressing government influence on platform moderation (Murthy v. Missouri, 2024) . Despite the significance of these interactions, the existing scholarly literature tends to focus on distinct but related dimensions: either platform regulation exclusively, examining the content of state-imposed obligations (for example, Husovec, 2024, among many others for the DSA, or Schulz, 2018 , for the now revoked NetzDG) or focusing on governance by platforms (DeNardis et al., 2015) , which is how platforms are developing their own policies and enforcing them (Gillespie, 2018; Roberts, 2019) , notably with the help of automated processes (Gorwa et al., 2020) . Less attention has been given to the nuanced forms of what Gorwa (2024) calls 'government intervention in content moderation'.

This paper aims to investigate state-platforms relationships by questioning the evolution of state involvement in content moderation over the years. Such an investigation is conducted through the lens of annual reports from the United Nations' Special Rapporteurs on freedom of expression. It provides an empirical and chronological perspective on the question of government intervention in content moderation, aiming to provide a grounded basis for transdisciplinary discussions on its implications for democracy and legality. United Nations' Special Rapporteurs (SRs) are independent experts from academia or civil society, elected by the UN General Assembly. With the administrative support of the Office of the High Commissioner on Human Rights, they document human rights problems and provide recommendations on a yearly basis. Considering their role at the crossroads between State authorities and civil society organizations, their reports offer a source for tracking trends and evolutions in states' actions and roles over the years. On this basis, our analysis makes two key contributions. First, it offers a chronological overview of how states have evolved in their positioning regarding content distributed online through the Internet. Second, it categorizes types of state-platform relationships, ranging from formal regulatory regimes to informal governmental influence. This categorization provides a useful framework for policymakers and scholars to assess transparency, human rights considerations, and democratic legitimacy (Haggart & Keller, 2021 ) within these interactions.

Understanding these relationships is particularly urgent, as social media companies increasingly have the potential to interfere with citizen's right to information and freedom of expression and impact electoral processes. State-platform collaborations can lack transparency, leading to concerns over accountability, the legitimacy of decision-making processes, and potential abuses of power. By empirically and chronologically mapping these relationships, this paper contributes to the ongoing debate on the relevance of regulatory approaches to social media platforms and on their possible blind spots. The paper proceeds as follows: Section 2 presents the existing literature on government intervention in social media platforms' content moderation. Section 3 constitutes the core of the analysis as it traces the chronological evolution of state involvement in online content moderation and proposes a framework to understand this evolution. Section 4 proposes a categorization of state-platform relationships to clarify their distinct forms, as well as discusses their geopolitical implications. Section 5 concludes by discussing the current backlash against platform regulation and the risks associated with state-platform collaborations in this context. Methodological details are provided in the annexes.

## Background: perspectives on states' involvement in content moderation

This section presents the literature on the issue of how governments are involved in content moderation processes. This literature is divided into two distinct categories based on the different perspectives they adopt regarding the question of the relationship between states and platforms. The first section (2.1.) presents works that explain how governments intervene in content moderation, adopting a descriptive stance on the interactions between states and platforms; the second section (2.2.) presents works that question this involvement, i.e., that discuss the legitimacy of certain interactions between states and platforms, often adopting a normative and critical stance.

## Explaining states' involvement in content moderation

Scholars have proposed various frameworks to explain state involvement in content moderation. Two of the most influential perspectives come from Gorwa (2024) and Balkin (2014 Balkin ( , 2018a Balkin ( , 2018b)) . Whereas Gorwa provides a structured typology of governmental intervention strategies, Balkin offers a conceptual model that redefines the regulatory dynamics among states, platforms, and users. Gorwa (2024) develops the most detailed framework, which he terms government intervention in content moderation. In his approach, he assumes that governments have a political will to shape how platforms moderate online content. From this premise, Gorwa identifies three key strategies that states can employ (Gorwa, 2024, pp. 60-65) . First, contesting occurs when a government directly opposes and seeks to change platform moderation, typically through direct regulation, that includes a 'system of sanctions and enforcement' and whose rules are developed by a public body. Second, collaboration refers to cooperative efforts among governments, platforms, and other stakeholders to influence content moderation. This approach is often less formal than direct regulation, although it can be codified in law. An example is the development of voluntary codes of conduct within the EU.
